claim: Extracellular electrophysiology and two-photon calcium imaging are widely used methods for measuring physiological activity with single-cell resolution across large populations of cortical neurons.
source: Extracellular electrophysiology and two-photon calcium imaging are widely used methods for measuring physiological activity with single-cell resolution across large populations of cortical neurons.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of neuroscience methods, drawing from established scientific knowledge.

claim: A larger fraction of responsive neurons is observed in electrophysiology compared to calcium imaging across all stimulus conditions tested.
source: Across all stimulus conditions tested, we observe a larger fraction of responsive neurons in electrophysiology and higher stimulus selectivity in calcium imaging, which was partially reconciled by applying a spikes-to-calcium forward model to the electrophysiology data.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data comparing the two modalities, as shown in the results section.

claim: Higher stimulus selectivity is observed in calcium imaging compared to electrophysiology across all stimulus conditions tested.
source: Across all stimulus conditions tested, we observe a larger fraction of responsive neurons in electrophysiology and higher stimulus selectivity in calcium imaging, which was partially reconciled by applying a spikes-to-calcium forward model to the electrophysiology data.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data comparing the two modalities, as shown in the results section.

claim: Applying a spikes-to-calcium forward model to electrophysiology data partially reconciles differences in responsiveness and selectivity between the two modalities.
source: Across all stimulus conditions tested, we observe a larger fraction of responsive neurons in electrophysiology and higher stimulus selectivity in calcium imaging, which was partially reconciled by applying a spikes-to-calcium forward model to the electrophysiology data.
evidence: This claim is supported by the analysis performed using the forward model on the electrophysiology data.

claim: The forward model could only reconcile differences in responsiveness when restricted to neurons with low contamination and an event rate above a minimum threshold.
source: However, the forward model could only reconcile differences in responsiveness when restricted to neurons with low contamination and an event rate above a minimum threshold.
evidence: This claim is supported by the analysis of how different filtering criteria affect the reconciliation between modalities.

claim: Recent advances have made it possible to record simultaneously from thousands of neurons with electrophysiology.
source: Recent advances have made it possible to record simultaneously from thousands of neurons with electrophysiology (Jun et al., 2017; Siegle et al., 2021; Stringer et al., 2019a) or tens of thousands of neurons with calcium imaging (Sofroniew et al., 2016; Stringer et al., 2019b; Weisenburger et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published work demonstrating these capabilities.

claim: Recent advances have made it possible to record simultaneously from tens of thousands of neurons with calcium imaging.
source: Recent advances have made it possible to record simultaneously from thousands of neurons with electrophysiology (Jun et al., 2017; Siegle et al., 2021; Stringer et al., 2019a) or tens of thousands of neurons with calcium imaging (Sofroniew et al., 2016; Stringer et al., 2019b; Weisenburger et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published work demonstrating these capabilities.

claim: Neither electrophysiology nor calcium imaging provides a completely faithful picture of the underlying neural activity.
source: While insights gained from both methods have been invaluable to the field, it is clear that neither technique provides a completely faithful picture of the underlying neural activity.
evidence: This is an inference based on the known limitations of both techniques and the results of the comparison.

claim: Calcium imaging can easily target recordings to genetically defined cell types through restricted expression of calcium indicators.
source: Since the expression of calcium indicators can be restricted to genetically defined cell types, imaging can easily target recordings to specific sub-populations (Madisen et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published work on transgenic mouse lines.

claim: The ability to identify genetically or projection-defined cell populations in electrophysiology experiments is far more limited compared to imaging.
source: The ability to identify genetically or projection-defined cell populations in electrophysiology experiments is far more limited (Economo et al., 2018; Jia et al., 2019; Lima et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published work on the limitations of electrophysiology for cell type identification.

claim: Imaging offers the ability to reliably return to the same neurons over many days without the need to implant bulky hardware.
source: Both techniques have been adapted for chronic recordings, but imaging offers the ability to reliably return to the same neurons over many days without the need to implant bulky hardware (Peters et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published work on chronic imaging.

claim: Imaging captures structural, in addition to functional, data, allowing individual neurons to be precisely registered to tissue volumes from electron microscopy.
source: Furthermore, because imaging captures structural, in addition to functional, data, individual neurons can be precisely registered to tissue volumes from electron microscopy (Bock et al., 2011; Lee et al., 2016), in vitro brain slices (Ko et al., 2011), and potentially other ex vivo techniques such as in situ RNA profiling (Chen et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published work on cross-modal registration.

claim: The sources of extracellular spike waveforms are very difficult to localize with sufficient precision to enable direct cross-modal registration.
source: In contrast, the sources of extracellular spike waveforms are very difficult to localize with sufficient precision to enable direct cross-modal registration.
evidence: This is an inference based on the known limitations of electrophysiology spatial resolution.

claim: Multi-photon imaging typically yields data in a single plane tangential to the cortical surface.
source: Multi-photon imaging typically yields data in a single plane tangential to the cortical surface, and is limited to depths of <1 mm due to a combination of light scattering and absorption in tissue.
evidence: This is a statement about the technical characteristics of multi-photon imaging, based on established knowledge.

claim: Multi-photon imaging is limited to depths of <1 mm due to a combination of light scattering and absorption in tissue.
source: Multi-photon imaging typically yields data in a single plane tangential to the cortical surface, and is limited to depths of <1 mm due to a combination of light scattering and absorption in tissue.
evidence: This is a statement about the technical limitations of multi-photon imaging, based on established knowledge.

claim: Imaging of most subcortical structures requires physical destruction of more superficial tissues.
source: While multi-plane (Yang et al., 2016) and deep structure (Ouzounov et al., 2017) imaging are both areas of active research, imaging of most subcortical structures requires physical destruction of more superficial tissues (Dombeck et al., 2010; Feinberg and Meister, 2015; Skocek et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published work on deep tissue imaging.

claim: Linear probes provide simultaneous access to neurons in both cortex and subcortical structures.
source: Linear probes provide simultaneous access to neurons in both cortex and subcortical structures, but make it difficult to sample many neurons from the same cortical layer.
evidence: This is a statement about the spatial sampling characteristics of linear probes, based on established knowledge.

claim: Imaging is limited by the dwell time required to capture enough photons to distinguish physiological changes in fluorescence from noise.
source: Imaging is limited by the dwell time required to capture enough photons to distinguish physiological changes in fluorescence from noise (Svoboda and Yasuda, 2006), and the kinetics of calcium-dependent indicators additionally constrain the ability to temporally localize neural activity (Chen et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published work on the technical limitations of imaging.

claim: The kinetics of calcium-dependent indicators constrain the ability to temporally localize neural activity.
source: Imaging is limited by the dwell time required to capture enough photons to distinguish physiological changes in fluorescence from noise (Svoboda and Yasuda, 2006), and the kinetics of calcium-dependent indicators additionally constrain the ability to temporally localize neural activity (Chen et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published work on calcium indicator kinetics.

claim: Most imaging studies are based on data sampled at frame rates between 1 and 30 Hz.
source: While kilohertz-scale imaging has been achieved (Kazemipour et al., 2019; Zhang et al., 2019), most studies are based on data sampled at frame rates between 1 and 30 Hz.
evidence: This is a statement about the typical frame rates used in imaging studies, based on established knowledge and citations.

claim: Extracellular electrophysiology requires sampling rates of 20 kHz or higher to capture the action potential waveform shape.
source: In contrast, extracellular electrophysiology requires sampling rates of 20 kHz or higher, in order to capture the action potential waveform shape that is essential for accurate spike sorting.
evidence: This is a statement about the technical requirements of electrophysiology, based on established knowledge.

claim: High sampling rates allow extracellular electrophysiology to pin-point neural activity in time with sub-millisecond resolution.
source: High sampling rates allow extracellular electrophysiology to pin-point neural activity in time with sub-millisecond resolution, enabling analyses of fine-timescale synchronization across simultaneously recorded neural populations.
evidence: This is a statement about the temporal resolution of electrophysiology, based on established knowledge.

claim: Electrophysiology measures action potentials, which are believed to be the fundamental currency of neuronal communication and causation.
source: The fact that electrophysiology can measure action potentials—what we believe to be the fundamental currency of neuronal communication and causation—bestows upon it a more basic ontological status than on calcium imaging, which captures an indirect measure of a neuron's spike train.
evidence: This is a statement based on established neuroscience knowledge about the role of action potentials.

claim: Calcium imaging captures an indirect measure of a neuron's spike train.
source: The fact that electrophysiology can measure action potentials—what we believe to be the fundamental currency of neuronal communication and causation—bestows upon it a more basic ontological status than on calcium imaging, which captures an indirect measure of a neuron's spike train.
evidence: This is a statement based on established knowledge about what calcium imaging measures.

claim: There has been no comprehensive attempt to characterize how the choice of recording modality affects the inferred functional properties of neurons in sensory cortex.
source: To date, there has been no comprehensive attempt to characterize how the choice of recording modality affects the inferred functional properties of neurons in sensory cortex.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of the literature, based on the authors' review.

claim: The Allen Brain Observatory pipelines used standardized surgical methods, experimental steps, and physical geometry of recording rigs matched as closely as possible between imaging and electrophysiology.
source: These datasets were collected using standardized pipelines, such that the surgical methods, experimental steps, and physical geometry of the recording rigs were matched as closely as possible (Figure 1C,D).
evidence: This claim is supported by the description of the experimental methods and Figure 1C,D showing the pipelines and rigs.

claim: Only ~10% of neurons in the imaging dataset responded reliably to all four stimuli (drifting gratings, static gratings, natural scenes, and natural movies).
source: Our original study, based on imaging data alone, revealed that only ~10% of the neurons in the imaging dataset responded reliably to all four stimuli, while the largest class of neurons contained those that did not respond reliably to any of the stimuli.
evidence: This claim is supported by data from the previous imaging study (de Vries et al., 2020).

claim: The largest class of neurons in the imaging dataset contained those that did not respond reliably to any of the stimuli.
source: Our original study, based on imaging data alone, revealed that only ~10% of the neurons in the imaging dataset responded reliably to all four stimuli, while the largest class of neurons contained those that did not respond reliably to any of the stimuli.
evidence: This claim is supported by data from the previous imaging study (de Vries et al., 2020).

claim: Preference metrics are largely invariant across modalities.
source: We find that preference metrics are largely invariant across modalities.
evidence: This claim is supported by the comparison of preference metrics between the two datasets.

claim: Electrophysiology suggests that neurons show a higher degree of responsiveness compared to imaging.
source: However, in this dataset, electrophysiology suggests that neurons show a higher degree of responsiveness, while imaging suggests that responsive neurons show a higher degree of selectivity.
evidence: This claim is supported by the comparison of responsiveness metrics between the two datasets.

claim: Imaging suggests that responsive neurons show a higher degree of selectivity compared to electrophysiology.
source: However, in this dataset, electrophysiology suggests that neurons show a higher degree of responsiveness, while imaging suggests that responsive neurons show a higher degree of selectivity.
evidence: This claim is supported by the comparison of selectivity metrics between the two datasets.

claim: Differences between modalities could be reduced by lowering the amplitude threshold for valid ΔF/F events.
source: These differences could be reduced by lowering the amplitude threshold for valid ΔF/F events, applying a spikes-to-calcium forward model to the electrophysiology data (Deneux et al., 2016), or sub-selection of neurons based either on event rate or by contamination level (the likelihood that signal from other neurons is misattributed to the neurons under consideration).
evidence: This claim is supported by the analysis of how different event detection thresholds affect the comparison.

claim: Differences between modalities could be reduced by applying a spikes-to-calcium forward model to the electrophysiology data.
source: These differences could be reduced by lowering the amplitude threshold for valid ΔF/F events, applying a spikes-to-calcium forward model to the electrophysiology data (Deneux et al., 2016), or sub-selection of neurons based either on event rate or by contamination level (the likelihood that signal from other neurons is misattributed to the neurons under consideration).
evidence: This claim is supported by the analysis using the forward model and citation to the method.

claim: Differences between modalities could be reduced by sub-selection of neurons based on event rate.
source: These differences could be reduced by lowering the amplitude threshold for valid ΔF/F events, applying a spikes-to-calcium forward model to the electrophysiology data (Deneux et al., 2016), or sub-selection of neurons based either on event rate or by contamination level (the likelihood that signal from other neurons is misattributed to the neurons under consideration).
evidence: This claim is supported by the analysis of how filtering by event rate affects the comparison.

claim: Differences between modalities could be reduced by sub-selection of neurons based on contamination level.
source: These differences could be reduced by lowering the amplitude threshold for valid ΔF/F events, applying a spikes-to-calcium forward model to the electrophysiology data (Deneux et al., 2016), or sub-selection of neurons based either on event rate or by contamination level (the likelihood that signal from other neurons is misattributed to the neurons under consideration).
evidence: This claim is supported by the analysis of how filtering by contamination level affects the comparison.

claim: Extracellular electrophysiology predominantly captures the activity of highly active units while missing or merging low-firing-rate units.
source: This reconciliation reveals the respective biases of these two recording modalities, namely that extracellular electrophysiology predominantly captures the activity of highly active units while missing or merging low-firing-rate units, while calcium-indicator binding dynamics sparsify neural responses and supralinearly amplify spike bursts.
evidence: This is an inference based on the analysis of how different filtering criteria affect the comparison.

claim: Calcium-indicator binding dynamics sparsify neural responses and supralinearly amplify spike bursts.
source: This reconciliation reveals the respective biases of these two recording modalities, namely that extracellular electrophysiology predominantly captures the activity of highly active units while missing or merging low-firing-rate units, while calcium-indicator binding dynamics sparsify neural responses and supralinearly amplify spike bursts.
evidence: This is an inference based on the analysis of the forward model and event detection.

claim: The imaging dataset was collected using genetically encoded GCaMP6f under the control of specific Cre driver lines.
source: The imaging dataset was collected using genetically encoded GCaMP6f (Chen et al., 2013) under the control of specific Cre driver lines.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental methods used for the imaging dataset.

claim: The ephys dataset included wild-type mice and transgenic mice expressing channelrhodopsin or GCaMP6f.
source: The ephys dataset also made use of transgenic mice in addition to wild-type mice. These transgenic mice expressed either channelrhodopsin in specific inhibitory populations for identification using optotagging (see Siegle et al., 2021 for details), or GCaMP6f in specific excitatory or inhibitory populations (see Materials and methods).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental methods used for the ephys dataset.

claim: The analysis was limited to putative excitatory neurons from five cortical visual areas (V1, LM, AL, PM, and AM).
source: We limited our comparative analysis to putative excitatory neurons from five cortical visual areas (V1, LM, AL, PM, and AM).
evidence: This is a description of the data filtering criteria used in the analysis.

claim: After filtering, 41,578 neurons from 170 mice were included from the imaging dataset.
source: After this filtering step, we were left with 41,578 neurons from 170 mice in imaging, and 11,030 neurons from 52 mice in ephys.
evidence: This is a description of the sample size after filtering.

claim: After filtering, 11,030 neurons from 52 mice were included from the ephys dataset.
source: After this filtering step, we were left with 41,578 neurons from 170 mice in imaging, and 11,030 neurons from 52 mice in ephys.
evidence: This is a description of the sample size after filtering.

claim: For the ephys dataset, stimulus-evoked responses were computed using spike times identified by Kilosort2.
source: For the ephys dataset, stimulus-evoked responses were computed using the spike times identified by Kilosort2 (Pachitariu et al., 2016a; Stringer et al., 2019a).
evidence: This is a description of the data analysis methods used for the ephys dataset.

claim: Kilosort2 uses information in the extracellularly recorded voltage traces to find templates that fit the spike waveform shapes of all the units in the dataset.
source: Kilosort2 uses information in the extracellularly recorded voltage traces to find templates that fit the spike waveform shapes of all the units in the dataset, and assigns a template to each spike.
evidence: This is a description of how the Kilosort2 algorithm works, based on established knowledge.

claim: The process of spike sorting does not perfectly recover the true underlying spike times and has the potential to miss spikes or assign spikes to the wrong unit.
source: The process of 'spike sorting'—regardless of the underlying algorithm—does not perfectly recover the true underlying spike times, and has the potential to miss spikes (false negatives) or assign spikes (or noise waveforms) to the wrong unit (false positives).
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of spike sorting, based on established knowledge.

claim: For the imaging dataset, the magnitude of the response for a given trial was determined by summing the amplitudes of events that occurred during the stimulation interval.
source: Therefore, in our population imaging dataset, we calculated the trial response magnitude by summing the amplitudes of events that occurred during the stimulation interval (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is a description of the data analysis methods used for the imaging dataset.

claim: Events detected from 2P imaging data do not represent individual spikes, but rather are heavily biased towards indicating short bouts of high firing rate, for example bursting.
source: For the most part, the events that are detected from the 2P imaging data do not represent individual spikes, but rather are heavily biased towards indicating short bouts of high firing rate, for example bursting (Huang et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published work on the relationship between calcium events and spikes.

claim: There is rich information contained in the amplitudes of calcium events, which have a non-linear but on average monotonic relationship with the underlying number of true spikes within a window.
source: There is, however, rich information contained in the amplitudes of these events, which have a non-linear—albeit on average monotonic—relationship with the underlying number of true spikes within a window.
evidence: This is a statement about the relationship between calcium event amplitudes and spike counts, based on established knowledge.

claim: A neuron was deemed responsive to a particular stimulus type if its response reliability was greater than 25%.
source: We consider both neurons to be responsive to the drifting gratings stimulus class because they have a significant response (p < 0.05, compared to a distribution of activity taken during the epoch of spontaneous activity) on at least 25% of the trials of the preferred condition (the grating direction and temporal frequency that elicited the largest mean response) (de Vries et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a description of the responsiveness criterion used in the analysis.

claim: Lifetime sparseness is used as the primary selectivity metric because it is a general metric applicable to every stimulus type.
source: We use lifetime sparseness (Vinje and Gallant, 2000) as our primary selectivity metric, because it is a general metric that is applicable to every stimulus type.
evidence: This is a description of the choice of selectivity metric and its justification.

claim: Lifetime sparseness equals 0 if the neuron responds equivalently to all stimulus conditions, and one if the neuron only responds to a single condition.
source: It reflects the distribution of responses of a neuron across some stimulus space (e.g. natural scenes or drifting gratings), equaling 0 if the neuron responds equivalently to all stimulus conditions, and one if the neuron only responds to a single condition.
evidence: This is a description of how lifetime sparseness is interpreted, based on its mathematical definition.

claim: Across all areas and mouse lines, lifetime sparseness is highly correlated with orientation selectivity for drifting gratings (R = 0.8 for ephys, 0.79 for imaging).
source: Across all areas and mouse lines, lifetime sparseness is highly correlated with more traditional selectivity metrics, such as drifting gratings orientation selectivity (R = 0.8 for ephys, 0.79 for imaging; Pearson correlation), static gratings orientation selectivity (R = 0.79 for ephys, 0.69 for imaging), and natural scenes image selectivity (R = 0.85 for ephys, 0.95 for imaging).
evidence: This claim is supported by the correlation analysis performed on the data.

claim: Across all areas and mouse lines, lifetime sparseness is highly correlated with orientation selectivity for static gratings (R = 0.79 for ephys, 0.69 for imaging).
source: Across all areas and mouse lines, lifetime sparseness is highly correlated with more traditional selectivity metrics, such as drifting gratings orientation selectivity (R = 0.8 for ephys, 0.79 for imaging; Pearson correlation), static gratings orientation selectivity (R = 0.79 for ephys, 0.69 for imaging), and natural scenes image selectivity (R = 0.85 for ephys, 0.95 for imaging).
evidence: This claim is supported by the correlation analysis performed on the data.

claim: Across all areas and mouse lines, lifetime sparseness is highly correlated with natural scenes image selectivity (R = 0.85 for ephys, 0.95 for imaging).
source: Across all areas and mouse lines, lifetime sparseness is highly correlated with more traditional selectivity metrics, such as drifting gratings orientation selectivity (R = 0.8 for ephys, 0.79 for imaging; Pearson correlation), static gratings orientation selectivity (R = 0.79 for ephys, 0.69 for imaging), and natural scenes image selectivity (R = 0.85 for ephys, 0.95 for imaging).
evidence: This claim is supported by the correlation analysis performed on the data.

claim: Jensen–Shannon distance was used to quantify the disparity between the imaging and ephys distributions.
source: We pooled responsiveness, preference, and selectivity metrics for all of the neurons in a given visual area across experiments, and quantified the disparity between the imaging and ephys distributions using Jensen–Shannon distance.
evidence: This is a description of the statistical method used for comparison.

claim: Jensen–Shannon distance is equal to 0 for perfectly overlapping distributions, and one for completely non-overlapping distributions.
source: Jensen–Shannon distance is equal to 0 for perfectly overlapping distributions, and one for completely non-overlapping distributions, and falls in between these values for partially overlapping distributions.
evidence: This is a description of how Jensen–Shannon distance is interpreted, based on its mathematical definition.

claim: Across all areas and stimuli, the fraction of responsive neurons was higher in the ephys dataset than the imaging dataset.
source: Across all areas and stimuli, the fraction of responsive neurons was higher in the ephys dataset than the imaging dataset (Figure 2E).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Tuning preferences were consistent between the two modalities, including preferred temporal frequency.
source: We found tuning preferences to be consistent between the two modalities, including preferred temporal frequency (Figure 2F), preferred direction (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A), preferred orientation (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B), and preferred spatial frequency (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 2F and supplementary figures.

claim: Selectivity metrics, such as lifetime sparseness, were consistently higher in imaging than ephys.
source: Selectivity metrics, such as lifetime sparseness (Figure 2G), orientation selectivity (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D), and direction selectivity (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E), were consistently higher in imaging than ephys.
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 2G and supplementary figures.

claim: After resampling each dataset to match layer distributions, there was very little change in the overall distributions of responsiveness, preference, and selectivity metrics.
source: After resampling each dataset to match layer distributions (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B, see Materials and methods for details), we saw very little change in the overall distributions of responsiveness, preference, and selectivity metrics (Figure 2—figure supplement 2C–E), indicating that laminar sampling biases are likely not a key cause of the differences we observed between the modalities.
evidence: This claim is supported by the analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Laminar sampling biases are likely not a key cause of the differences observed between the modalities.
source: After resampling each dataset to match layer distributions (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B, see Materials and methods for details), we saw very little change in the overall distributions of responsiveness, preference, and selectivity metrics (Figure 2—figure supplement 2C–E), indicating that laminar sampling biases are likely not a key cause of the differences we observed between the modalities.
evidence: This is an inference based on the analysis of laminar sampling bias.

claim: Mice tend to spend a larger fraction of time running in the ephys experiments compared to imaging experiments.
source: In our datasets, mice tend to spend a larger fraction of time running in the ephys experiments, perhaps because of the longer experiment duration, which may be further confounded by genotype-specific differences in running behavior (Figure 2—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3A.

claim: Within each modality, running had a similar impact on visual response metrics.
source: Within each modality, running had a similar impact on visual response metrics.
evidence: This claim is supported by the analysis of running effects on response metrics.

claim: On average, units in ephys and neurons in imaging have slightly lower responsiveness during periods of running versus non-running.
source: On average, units in ephys and neurons in imaging have slightly lower responsiveness during periods of running versus non-running (Figure 2—figure supplement 3B), but slightly higher selectivity (Figure 2—figure supplement 3C).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3B.

claim: On average, units in ephys and neurons in imaging have slightly higher selectivity during periods of running versus non-running.
source: On average, units in ephys and neurons in imaging have slightly lower responsiveness during periods of running versus non-running (Figure 2—figure supplement 3B), but slightly higher selectivity (Figure 2—figure supplement 3C).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3C.

claim: Sub-sampling imaging experiments to match the overall distribution of running fraction to the ephys data had a negligible impact on responsiveness, selectivity, and preference metrics.
source: To control for the effect of running, we sub-sampled our imaging experiments in order to match the overall distribution of running fraction to the ephys data (Figure 2—figure supplement 4A). This transformation had a negligible impact on responsiveness, selectivity, and preference metrics (Figure 2—figure supplement 4B–D).
evidence: This claim is supported by the analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4.

claim: Behavioral differences do not account for the differences in functional properties inferred from imaging and ephys.
source: From this analysis we conclude that, at least for the datasets examined here, behavioral differences do not account for the differences in functional properties inferred from imaging and ephys.
evidence: This is an inference based on the analysis of behavioral effects.

claim: Scientific conclusions can depend on both the method of event extraction and the chosen parameters.
source: Prior work has shown that scientific conclusions can depend on both the method of event extraction and the chosen parameters (Evans et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published work on event extraction methods.

claim: The exact ℓ0 method had a low rate of false positives (8 ± 2% in 100 ms bins).
source: We found that the exact ℓ0 method, which includes a built-in sparsity constraint, had a low rate of false positives (8 ± 2% in 100 ms bins, N = 32 ground truth recordings), whereas NND had a much higher rate (21 ± 4%; p = 8e-7, Wilcoxon signed-rank test).
evidence: This claim is supported by the analysis of ground truth data.

claim: NND had a much higher rate of false positives (21 ± 4%) compared to exact ℓ0.
source: We found that the exact ℓ0 method, which includes a built-in sparsity constraint, had a low rate of false positives (8 ± 2% in 100 ms bins, N = 32 ground truth recordings), whereas NND had a much higher rate (21 ± 4%; p = 8e-7, Wilcoxon signed-rank test).
evidence: This claim is supported by the analysis of ground truth data.

claim: Small-amplitude false positive events have very little impact on the overall correlation between the ground truth spike rate and the extracted events.
source: Small-amplitude false positive events have very little impact on the overall correlation between the ground truth spike rate and the extracted events, so parameter optimization does not typically penalize such events.
evidence: This is an inference based on the analysis of event extraction performance.

claim: The summation of many false positive events could have a noticeable impact on response magnitudes averaged over trials.
source: However, we reasoned that the summation of many false positive events could have a noticeable impact on response magnitudes averaged over trials.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the observation of false positive events.

claim: Applying a minimum-amplitude threshold to the event time series obtained via NND resulted in almost no change in the correlation between event amplitude and the ground truth firing rate.
source: As expected, this procedure resulted in almost no change in the correlation between event amplitude and the ground truth firing rate (Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by the analysis shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Applying a minimum-amplitude threshold to the event time series obtained via NND had a noticeable impact on both the average response magnitude within a given time window and the false positive rate.
source: However, it had a noticeable impact on both the average response magnitude within a given time window (Figure 3C), as well as the false positive rate (Figure 3D).
evidence: This claim is supported by the analysis shown in Figure 3C and 3D.

claim: Extracting events from a population dataset using NND resulted in much lower measured overall selectivity levels, even lower than for electrophysiology.
source: Extracting events from a population dataset (N = 3095 Slc17a7+ neurons from V1) using NND resulted in much lower measured overall selectivity levels, even lower than for electrophysiology (Figure 3F).
evidence: This claim is supported by the analysis shown in Figure 3F.

claim: A threshold between 3 and 4σ brought the selectivity distribution closest to the ephys distribution.
source: Thresholding out events at multiples of each neuron's noise level (σ) raised selectivity levels; a threshold between 3 and 4σ brought the selectivity distribution closest to the ephys distribution, while a threshold between 4 and 5σ resulted in selectivity that roughly matched that obtained with exact ℓ0 (Figure 2G).
evidence: This claim is supported by the analysis shown in Figure 3F.

claim: A threshold between 4 and 5σ resulted in selectivity that roughly matched that obtained with exact ℓ0.
source: Thresholding out events at multiples of each neuron's noise level (σ) raised selectivity levels; a threshold between 3 and 4σ brought the selectivity distribution closest to the ephys distribution, while a threshold between 4 and 5σ resulted in selectivity that roughly matched that obtained with exact ℓ0 (Figure 2G).
evidence: This claim is supported by the analysis shown in Figure 3F.

claim: The rate of low-amplitude events also affected responsiveness metrics.
source: The rate of low-amplitude events also affected responsiveness metrics (Figure 3G).
evidence: This claim is supported by the analysis shown in Figure 3G.

claim: Responsiveness was highest when all detected events were included, matching or slightly exceeding the levels measured with ephys.
source: Responsiveness was highest when all detected events were included, matching or slightly exceeding the levels measured with ephys.
evidence: This claim is supported by the analysis of responsiveness as a function of event threshold.

claim: Applying an amplitude threshold between 4 and 5σ brought responsiveness to the level originally measured with exact ℓ0.
source: Again, applying an amplitude threshold between 4 and 5σ brought responsiveness to the level originally measured with exact ℓ0.
evidence: This claim is supported by the analysis of responsiveness as a function of event threshold.

claim: Altering the 2P event extraction methodology represents one possible avenue for reconciling results from imaging and ephys.
source: This analysis demonstrates that altering the 2P event extraction methodology represents one possible avenue for reconciling results from imaging and ephys.
evidence: This is an inference based on the analysis of event extraction methods.

claim: Different parameters were needed to reconcile either selectivity or responsiveness, and the optimal parameters further depend on the presented stimulus class.
source: However, as different parameters were needed to reconcile either selectivity or responsiveness, and the optimal parameters further depend on the presented stimulus class, this cannot be the whole story.
evidence: This is an inference based on the analysis of event extraction parameters.

claim: All three proteins (Cre, tTA, and GCaMP6f) have been shown to have neurotoxic effects under certain conditions.
source: All three proteins have been shown to have neurotoxic effects under certain conditions (Han et al., 2012; Schmidt-Supprian and Rajewsky, 2007; Steinmetz et al., 2017), and calcium indicators, which by design bind intracellular calcium, can additionally interfere with cellular signaling pathways.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published work on the effects of these proteins.

claim: Calcium indicators can interfere with cellular signaling pathways.
source: All three proteins have been shown to have neurotoxic effects under certain conditions (Han et al., 2012; Schmidt-Supprian and Rajewsky, 2007; Steinmetz et al., 2017), and calcium indicators, which by design bind intracellular calcium, can additionally interfere with cellular signaling pathways.
evidence: This is a statement based on established knowledge about calcium indicators.

claim: Electrophysiology was performed in mice that expressed GCaMP6f under the control of specific Cre drivers.

source: One possibility is that there may be residual undetected contamination in our ephys recordings. An ISI violations score of 0 does not guarantee that there is no contamination, just that we are not able to measure it using this metric.

evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published work on forward model fitting.

source: We strove to mitigate this shortcoming by showing that brute-force exploration of MLSpike model parameter space could not significantly improve the match between real and synthetic imaging data.

evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published work on probe-induced activity.

source: Careful simultaneous measurements will be required in order to account for this relative activity increase.
evidence: This is a recommendation for future work.

source: While results obtained from ephys and imaging are sometimes treated as if they were interchangeable from a scientific standpoint, in actuality they each provide related but fundamentally different perspectives on the underlying neural activity.
evidence: This is a statement about how results from the two modalities are sometimes treated in the literature.

source: Extracellular electrophysiology tells us—with sub-millisecond temporal resolution—about a neuron's spiking output.
evidence: This is a statement about what electrophysiology measures, based on established knowledge.

source: Calcium imaging doesn't measure the outgoing action potentials directly, but rather the impact of input and output signals on a neuron's internal state, in terms of increases in calcium concentration that drive various downstream pathways (West et al., 2001).

evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published work on voltage indicators.

source: A recent study comparing matched populations recorded with electrophysiology or imaging emphasized differences in the temporal profiles of spike trains and calcium-dependent fluorescence responses (Wei et al., 2019).

source: The authors found that event-extraction algorithms that convert continuous ΔF/F traces to putative spike times could not recapitulate the temporal profiles measured with electrophysiology; on the other hand, a forward model that transformed spike times to synthetic ΔF/F traces could make their electrophysiology results appear more like those from the imaging experiments.

claim: A forward model that transformed spike times to synthetic ΔF/F traces could make electrophysiology results appear more like those from imaging experiments.
source: The authors found that event-extraction algorithms that convert continuous ΔF/F traces to putative spike times could not recapitulate the temporal profiles measured with electrophysiology; on the other hand, a forward model that transformed spike times to synthetic ΔF/F traces could make their electrophysiology results appear more like those from the imaging experiments.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published work (Wei et al., 2019).

source: However, there are other types of functional metrics that are not explicitly dependent on temporal factors, such as responsiveness, which cannot be reconciled using a forward model alone.
evidence: This is an inference based on the findings of the current study.

source: It is worth emphasizing that we are not suggesting that researchers use the methods we describe here to attempt to make all of their imaging data more similar to electrophysiological data, or vice versa.
evidence: This is a clarification of the authors' intent.

source: Since no one single method is intrinsically superior to the other, doing so would merely introduce additional biases.
evidence: This is a statement about the relative merits of the two modalities.

claim: The authors recommend that readers examine how sensitive their chosen functional metrics are to signal contamination, application of a forward model, filtering by event rate, and false positives during event detection.
source: Instead, we recommend that readers examine how sensitive their chosen functional metrics, and, by extension, their derived scientific conclusions are to (1) signal contamination during spike detection and sorting (for electrophysiology data), (2) application of a spike-to-calcium forward model (for electrophysiology data), (3) filtering by event rate (for imaging data), and (4) false positives introduced during event detection (for imaging data).
evidence: This is a recommendation based on the findings of the study.

source: If the chosen functional metrics are found to be largely insensitive to the above transformations, then results can be compared directly across studies that employ different recording modalities.

evidence: This is a statement about the need for future work.

claim: One approach currently underway is to carry out recordings with extremely high-density silicon probes (Neuropixels Ultra), over 10x denser than the Neuropixels 1.0 probes used in this study.
source: One approach, currently underway at the Allen Institute and elsewhere, is to carry out recordings with extremely high-density silicon probes (Neuropixels Ultra), over 10x denser (in terms of the number of electrodes per unit of area) than the Neuropixels 1.0 probes used in this study.
evidence: This is a description of ongoing work.

claim: High-density probes can capture each spike waveform with 100 or more electrodes, making it easier to disambiguate waveforms from nearby neurons.
source: Such probes can capture each spike waveform with 100 or more electrodes, making it easier to disambiguate waveforms from nearby neurons, and making it less likely that neurons with small somata would evade detection or that their waveforms would be mistaken for those of other units.
evidence: This is a statement about the expected benefits of high-density probes.

claim: High-density probe experiments should make it easier to quantify the selection bias of extracellular electrophysiology.
source: These experiments should make it easier to quantify the selection bias of extracellular electrophysiology, as well as the degree to which missed neurons and contaminated spike trains have influenced the results of the current study.
evidence: This is a statement about the expected benefits of high-density probe experiments.

source: In addition, experiments in which silicon probes are combined with two-photon imaging—either through interleaved sampling, spike-triggered image acquisition, or improved artifact removal techniques—could provide more direct ground-truth information about the relationship between extracellular electrophysiology and calcium imaging.
evidence: This is a statement about the expected benefits of combined probe and imaging experiments.

source: The fact that functional metrics are sensitive not only to experimental procedures but also to data processing steps and cell inclusion criteria (Mesa et al., 2021), makes it difficult to directly compare results across studies.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published work.

source: Having access to ephys and imaging datasets collected under largely identical conditions allowed us to rule out a number of potential confounds, such as laminar sampling bias and inter-modality behavioral differences.
evidence: This is a statement about the benefits of the standardized datasets used in the study.

evidence: This is a statement about the future role of simultaneous ephys/imaging experiments.

source: Ultimately, the goal of this work is not to establish the superiority of any one recording modality in absolute terms, since their complementary strengths ensure they will each remain essential to scientific progress for many years to come.
evidence: This is a statement about the authors' goals.

evidence: This is a conclusion based on the findings of the study.

source: Selectivity metrics based on spike counts (the neuron's outputs) will almost always be lower than selectivity metrics based on calcium concentrations (the neuron's internal state).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the findings of the study.

source: Even with this in mind, however, we cannot fully reproduce the observed levels of calcium-dependent selectivity using spike times alone—suggesting that a neuron's internal state may contain stimulus-specific information that is not necessarily reflected in its outputs.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the findings of the study.

source: We have attempted to account for these biases by (1) altering 2P event detection parameters, (2) applying sub-selection to account for built-in spatial biases, and (3) simulating calcium signals via a forward model.
evidence: This is a summary of the methods used in the study.

evidence: This is a conclusion based on the findings of the study.

source: For example, to what degree does the bias of ephys for higher-firing-rate units stem from the recording hardware versus the spike sorting procedure? It is possible that more spatially precise sampling, or modifications to the spike sorting algorithm, will reduce this bias in the future.

source: Similarly, how much of the 2P imaging bias stems from the calcium indicator versus the event extraction algorithm? New indicators (such as GCaMP8) may ameliorate some of these problems, as could further optimization of the event extraction step.
